title: The Yaksha's question at the lake
word: with the Keeper's framing of what
hookLine: when the books run out, Yudhishthira points to the path of the good
carry: when scripture is silent, the good decide
tomorrow: why would a handbook on power open with a bow?
last: KNOWLEDGE FROM A TEACHER REACHES ITS GOAL.

lines: THE ONE THE GREAT HAVE WALKED.
cards: Four brothers lie dead beside a forest lake. Each one drank without answering the voice that guards the water. The fifth brother, Yudhishthira, comes thirsty to the same shore, and the voice speaks again.
It's a yaksha, a spirit of the lake. Answer my questions first, it says. So he does, question after question, and one of them is this: what is the path?

His answer is one of the most quoted lines in the Mahabharata. In paraphrase: reasoning is unsteady, the scriptures differ, and no single sage's word is final. The truth of dharma is hidden in a cave.
So the path is the one the great have walked.

teach.b: The yaksha, it turns out, is Dharma himself, and he brings the brothers back. But the answer is the part Hindus still live by.

teach.h: SADACHARA: THE CONDUCT OF THE GOOD.
teach.b: The scriptures can't name every case, so the dharma books count more than one root of dharma: the Veda, the remembered texts, sadachara, the conduct of good people, and the heart's own contentment.
The Manusmriti, near its end, turns this into a method. In paraphrase: for points of dharma the book hasn't covered, what the learned, the shishtas, declare shall have force.
It even sketches a parishad, a small gathering of people who know the Veda and can reason, and says what they settle is dharma.
Then a warning: a crowd that doesn't know and doesn't keep the vows can't make dharma, however many gather.
That's why, when a Hindu family meets a new question, a puja streamed to cousins abroad, a ritual in a new country, it rarely takes a vote.

It asks the pandit, the elder who keeps the rites, the people whose lives show they know. Who gets a seat in that circle has been argued for centuries; reformers like Vidyasagar and Ambedkar pressed that question hard.

teach.h: WHEN THE BOOK IS SILENT, LOOK TO THE GOOD.
teach.b: When the book is silent, look to the good, weighing together.

how: When the old books don't answer a new question, Hindu families usually ask a pandit, a learned teacher or the elders who keep the rites; temples and gatherings of scholars weigh the harder questions together.

games.q: what does “with the keeper's framing of what” mean?
o: a ruling that throws a whole old book away for good
where the dharma books send a question they never answered
a fixed list of rules that no reader may ever question

games.q: when the books are silent — tap the pairs.
p: the path is the one the great have walked
the conduct of good people, a root of dharma
a small gathering that settles open questions

s: Yudhishthira told the yaksha that reasoning alone settles dharma
he said reasoning is unsteady and the scriptures differ; the path is the one the great have walked.
the Manusmriti says a big enough crowd can settle dharma
it warns the opposite: a crowd without learning can't make dharma, however many gather.
it names a parishad, a small assembly, for open questions
people who know the Veda and can reason; what they settle is dharma, the book says.

games.q: your temple's committee has no rule on whether to livestream the evening aarti. one member wants a show of hands from everyone in the lobby after the service. by the Manusmriti's last chapter, what settles it?
o: the lobby vote. the more people, the surer the answer.
a small group who know the rites and can reason, weighing it together.
nothing. if the old books have no rule, the question can't be answered.
games.why: when the books are silent, Hindu tradition looks to the good: a parishad of a few who know and can reason. it warns that a crowd alone, however big, can't make dharma.

practice: Bring to mind one elder or teacher whose life shows you what dharma looks like. If you pray, bow to them silently, the way many Hindus touch an elder's feet. If you don't, write their name slowly on paper or in a notes app.
Then rest your eyes, and let your breath settle while you hold them in mind.

wordCard.voice: Parishad: a small gathering of the learned, the circle the Manusmriti trusts with the questions its pages never answer.

orig.note: Sanskrit parishad, an assembly: the gathering the Manusmriti trusts with open questions.

carryVoice: Keep this: when scripture is silent, the good decide. Yudhishthira pointed the way at the lake. That closes this stretch.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Aranyaka (Vana) Parva, the Yaksha's questions at the lake (3.297 in the critical edition; 3.313 in the vulgate): 'what is the path?' answered with reasoning unsteady, scriptures differing, dharma hidden in a cave, the path the great have walked; the yaksha revealed as Dharma
Manusmriti 2.6 and 2.12 (the roots and marks of dharma: Veda, smriti, the conduct of the good, the self's contentment)
